blocks.x: It's working Papa, you know. Papa Lane? Yeah it's working. Yeah I got it working now. So I want to put today's date on here if I can. What's today's date? 25th. April the 25th 1963. 64. 64 yeah.
Nothing wrong with updating all of them dates.
Yeah. Yeah and we're making this at... Nothing wrong. Where are we located Papa? Huh? What's the address here?
421 Hesper, Metro Louisiana.
Yeah. You were going to tell us about the Wild West show?

Yes. Well, this is a coincidence that happened to me. I had a man, young man, playing tuba. His name was Joe Cascaro. And one day he took seriously sick. Now that evening he sent me word that he wasn't able to come down to play music with me and play us at this Wild West showcase. Well here I wasn't a terrible fix. Well a friend of mine, I thought of the Chinaman, Martin. I runs up to Casco and I borrow his tuba. And I give the tuba to this boy to play. He said to me, I don't know nothing about... I said you shove that in your face and play it. That's all. I don't know nothing about tuba. So we played them jobs. We finished that contract. I finished that contract. And it was a fellow by the name of O'Brien, young Buffalo Bill. Young Buffalo Bill. Young Buffalo Bill. Yes, he had that show. So we played, went down the corner, we played, went back to the lot.
This was a marching band? Marching band? Marching band. Marching band.

Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. Marching band. He said he was a champion. I'll tell you that's right. But I'll be there. He pumped on that tuba remarkably. And I took notice to it. And I said to him, say, boy, I said, why don't you get yourself a good tuba? He said, I believe I will. So I think he went and got one of them hurricanes. They were like a bretter, you know, you put over your head. Yeah. It was a double-E flat. A double-B flat, that's what it was. So he went and got one of them. I think he bought a second-handed. And he said, I'm going to play tuba from now on. I said, I wish you would. He said, I can put my hand on you at any minute. I won't have to run around for the jet fellas. So sure enough, he did. He learnt that tuba. And I mean, he turned out to be wonderful. Wonderful. Wonderful. What was his full name, Papa?

Martin Abraham. Martin Abraham. Yeah. Well, we call him Chink Martin. Chink Martin? Yeah. Yeah. Uh, Papa, let's get everybody's name down here. What's your name? Bill Stuckey. And your name? My name. Yeah, don't you know your name? Oh, yeah. That's what it is. You're Mrs. Lane, huh? Mrs. Lane, yeah. Mrs. Blanche Lane, huh? Yeah. And I'm Dick Allen. You want to hear it back now, Papa? Well, I'd like to. I'll see how it's found. All right. What did you think of that, Papa? Pretty good. Pretty good, huh? Papa, can I ask you a question or two? Can I ask you a question or two? Most anything in the world. All right, sir. I believe you said you were 91 years old. That's right. Do you know of any of the old musicians that are still living who are older than you are? No, not a one. As far as you know, you're about the oldest one. Not a one, but I know. Mm-hmm. What about the straight men? What about the straight men? Are there any of them living? The guys that played the straight stuff.
Straight jobs?
Yeah, you know straight music, readers.

Yeah, but I don't know any of them anymore. They're all passed away. Is that right? They're all passed away. Every one of them is passed away. Yeah, I don't know. Every one of them. There's bolden. There's brown. All of them. They're all passed away.
And he was older than any of them. You was older than any of them. You was older than any of them.
In the band?
You was older than any of the other fellas.
Were you older than Gilles Rouge? The old musicians? No. No. Who was older than you? They were older than me. Who? Braun and Secrets and all them guys. They were older than me.
Yeah, I didn't know that.
What about Dave Perkins? Yes, way older than me.
And Perkins?
What about Perkins? Dave Perkins? Dave Perkins was an older man than me.
Yeah.
How much? I believe Dave was about eight years or seven years older than me. Seven years older than I was.
What about Barquet? How old was he?
Barquet was just around about my age. What about Gilles Rouge?
Who? The piccolo player, Gilles Rouge. Gilles. Gilles Rouge.
Gilles. Gilles Rouge. No, Gilles. Gilles. Gilles Rouge. Don't you know?
Oh, Gilles Rouge, the piccolo player? Yeah.
Piccolo player.
Oh, he was about then. Gilles Rouge was about then, well, I'd say about 18.
And how old would you be? How old would you be? About the same age. About the same age. Yeah. About the same age. I don't think. How old were you when you learned how to play the drums?

Oh, I guess. I used to fool at them things when I was just brought up. I think they walked. When the Cotton Exposition came down here, the Sugar and Cotton Exposition, I'm speaking about that, it was way back in 1885. Way back in there. Way back in 1885. My old man happened to buy a drum up there. You know, one of them field drums. There weren't no kettle drums, it was field drums. And he brought it down to me. And then I was about 20 years old, and he made me a present of it. See? And then from then on, I kept on going with the drums until I reorganized. At first, I had a regular field band. Is that right? With Gil Rouge and Perkman. Oh, a few of the boys, you know. Coming to the kids, made the man in the valley pickaloos. The tin flute for a nickel. And I did pretty good.
How old were you when you first started playing for money? For money? Yeah.
Oh, around about 14, I played a political parade. Political parade. Yeah.
Was that after the Cotton Exposition? Oh, yeah.
That was about two years after the Cotton Exposition.
That was after the Cotton Exposition.
Oh, yes. That was after. Oh, yes. Yeah. Oh, I wasn't playing music for money during that time. No. Uh-uh.

Well, Papa, let me ask you this. What kind of music were you playing when you first started playing for money? What kind of music was it? Drums. Mm-hmm. Trap drums, a little bit alto, and bass fiddle. What kind of tunes did your band play?
What?
What kind of tunes did y'all play?
What kind of music? What kind of songs did you play?

What kind of songs? Mm-hmm. Well, all of our own composition. Your own composition? Yes. We had one man by the very, uh, Lawrence Vega and this part of Parquet. Well, in fact, the rest of them boys, they'd be with them all kinds of funny stuff. The first thing you know, when they'd get into the house with me and a bunch of kids, they'd want to try to see if they could play that stuff over again. Mm-hmm. And sure enough, they used us. Now, there was this Liberty Stable Blues, they call it. Liberty Stable Blues? Yeah. We, we, uh, Parquet composed that. Ah, S.H.I.E.L.D. Barquet, that one? Yes, sir. Yes, sir. Him and Yellow Nunez.
Mm-hmm.
Yes, sir. We used to call that, um, uh, let me tell you who's, we used to call that again. Yeah. Well, we had, we gave it different funny names.
I understand. I know, you told me about that before.
Yes.
Like florens and meatballs and numbers like that.

That's it, all that sort of stuff, see? Him give it different funny names, you know. So this fellow Edwards, goes up in New York. Mm-hmm. They've sent for me to go up there, and I wouldn't go up there because I had plenty of contracts down here, and I didn't want to go out of the city. I wanted to fill them contracts.
Papa, was this when you were 14? Was this when you were 14? Oh, no. No, this was later. That's later. Oh, later.
This was later.
This was in the 1910s. Oh, I see.

So anyhow, he got up there and he started to play. There wasn't such a thing during my time as records. There was nothing like that. Right. So he had this plowereen played, and he called it Liberty Stable Blues. Mm-hmm. And he took the credit for it. But that was brought in from Yellow Nunes and Bacquet.

Well, Yellow sued him, you know that. Yellow sued him. Yellow sued him. Tell him Yellow sued him. Yellow sued him. Took him to court. Yellow took him to court. Yellow. Oh, that song, yeah. Oh, yeah. He's dead. No, years ago. Years ago. He can't hear it. I don't know what you say.
Yellow sued Edwards for that on account of that same piece, you see, when he was up in New York.
Yeah.
Took him to court.
Don't you remember? I kind of remember. Yeah, Yellow sent and told us about it. Oh, yeah, they come to me. Yeah, Yellow told us, yeah.
That's it. They come to me. And I told them. Only two men. Yellow, Nunes, and Bacquet.
Yeah.

Papa, I'd like to hear you talk some more about that music that you played when you were 14, when you first started playing for money. Yeah. Did you say you played this livery stable blues then? Yeah. We played all that stuff.
Powering, livery stable blues, midnight show, all that sort of stuff. Ask them if it was by ear or from the music. All that stuff.
Oh, it must have been by ear. You never played by music, none of that. That was by ear, eh?
All by ear. All by ear.
You didn't play the livery stable blues and meatballs and all that when you was 14, though.
Well, if I played it after that, yes, I played it after that.
When you was 14 years old?
Well, I had parquet and all that.
Well, you had parquet and poikens and them, weren't you? Well, of course.
Yeah, but...
But that wasn't when you were 14, huh? Huh?

No. But that was not when you were 14? Not when I was 14. But that's how I began to play street marches and stuff like that. I see. Then we played that orchestra stuff. All kinds of stuff for orchestra. I asked him what he played when he was 14. The dancing and so on and so on. Weddings and stuff like that. Right. Balls and stuff like that. Well...
Well, let me ask you this. What did you call this music? You didn't use the word ragtime, did you? You didn't call it ragtime, did you? Called it ragtime. You called it ragtime. When you were 14?

When you were 14? Yes. When I was 14, that was the name of that stuff. Ragtime. Ragtime. No other name. We used to play all that kind of humbug stuff with them picaloos and stuff, you understand? Yes. When I was 14. Mm-hmm. See? Well, it... It happened, we used to go around the street with a bunch of kids. Flags and torch lights and stuff like that playing. Every night we'd be out in the street playing music. And marching. Making money out of it? No. No, just having fun. Just for pleasure. Uh-huh. So, Dr. George Howard's daddy, he came to me one time, there was a political rally. And he came to me, heard me playing, we lived right around the corner of him. Heard me with them kids, you know, all playing, one thing or another. They asked me that I'd like to come out with them and play. It was a regular parade, political parade. Oh, I said, yeah, sure. Now, don't you know, I brought out about 10 men, about 10 boys. And we played that parade. And we played that parade. And that man gave me $33. $33. That's what they gave me.
Do you remember who was running for office?

No, I don't remember. Was that a city election? Yes, it was a city election. Because I don't remember who was running for office or anything. I don't know. But it was during the time of the CLs and the regulars and those different organizations like that were all mixed up.
Right. Now, the music that y'all played didn't have any name, right? You were just improvised? You just made up the music as you went along? Yes, we went along. You didn't have any name?

As we went along, we made it up. Now, you believe me or not, and this is a got of mine is truth. Whenever I got out on the street after I had the band going all right, they had all kind of little nigga kids following us from the time we started parade until we finished on the street. Sure. Following the parade. Following the band. All kind of...
and killing.
By God, it's wonderful. Can you remember how any of those tunes go that you played at that political parade? Can you hum any of them?
Well, not in particular, but there's one of them that had a break in it. La la. La la. La La
La I say, if you syncopate a march, it comes out a rag. That's all. Yeah. You play a march hard, it's a rag.

Now, we used to play that underarm march. That was a wonderful march. Dave Perkins came down one night with a copy of that. And Dave Perkins was a first-class note reader. Really. That boy could take a sheet of music and go over it like nobody's business. Is that right? Well, he'd hum it. He'd hum it to the bunch. And the kids, man, they said they had a ear for music. Every one of them. Every one of them had a ear for music. Well, first thing you know, they start. They play this stuff, try to play it. Then he tried to manage to teach them and show them, you know. Well, we went along. Now, we used to play that underarm march. Underarm march is the name of it? Underarm.
Yeah.
Underarm. That's on sheet.
Underarm.
Underarm.
I see.
That's the name of the march. Then we played another march. Nethermarch is something about the American flag or something like that. I can't remember that stuff no more. It's been too long.
Right. Ask him if he ever heard the Stars and Stripes forever. I can't remember it. Did you ever hear the Stars and Stripes forever? Yes. We played that. You did? We played that. Did you rag it up?
Yes, we rag it up. We tear it up. Yes, we tear it up. Could dance. All of that stuff, that straight stuff, you understand? Right. All that straight stuff, we'd rag it up.
Of course, we should go. Well, I'll be there.
I mean, we should go. Yeah.
And that was for the political meeting that you played when you were 14. Yeah.
Well, actually, good after I was 14, I was around, I must have been close to 15 years old. I see. I must have been close to 15 years old when that happened.
Let me ask you this, Papa. Do you recall, when was it when you heard your first rag? When did you hear the first rag you ever heard in your life? First rag I ever heard in my life? Yeah.

Were you a little baby or a kid or? Oh, no. No, no. I was around the time when I used to play around with the kids around about, well, when I lived next door to Lynn's. That's before we were, long before we were married. I must have been about eight years old. Eight years old?

I must have been about eight years old. That would have been about 1881? Seven like that. Seven like that. You don't remember the name of the first rag. I don't guess you would. No, I don't. What about cakewalks? Ask him if you heard any cakewalks. How about cakewalks? You hear many cakewalks. No, we used to play it, but then it was out before I played it. I see. It was out before you were able to play? Yeah. No. Ask him. No, we were playing music. What do you mean out? If it was out of style? No, no. If it was published and out.
The cakewalk was before you started to play? No, no. No, no.

That was after. Cakewalk came out, was published after you started to play it. Yeah. What about coon songs, Mama? What about coon? The cakewalk came after. What about coon songs? Coon songs. How about coon songs? Coon songs. Coon songs. Yeah. You ever heard that word? They had songs like, If the Man and the Moon Were a Coon. No, I never. You never played those kind of songs. Let me ask you this, Papa. This Dave Perkins, he taught you how to play? No. No, he didn't? No. Picked that up myself. Oh, I see. Well, Dave Perkins, was he a rag musician? Yes, and a good one. Good one. Was he? A young man like myself was. I see. Do you know whether or not they were playing rags before you were born? No, I wouldn't know that. You don't know?

You never heard anybody talk about that? Well, I heard ragtime mentioned, ragtime music mentioned, time and time again. When you were a very, very young child? Yeah. Not young child, no. I was around about, like I say, 18 years old.

About nine years old, yeah. About 18, 19, 18 years old. I heard about that ragtime, yeah. Was that similar to what they call Dixieland today? I asked him if it was similar to Dixieland today. Was that a lot like what we call Dixieland today? No. Was that like, no, it wasn't like Dixieland? No. What was it like? What? What did it sound like? The music?

Yeah. Sounded pretty good to me. It sounded to everybody because I'll quickly tell you. When I organized the band, it seems like, I don't know whether they liked the music or not, but it engaged me three, four, and five months ahead of time to play music for them. I prayed for the ladies of Violet from down below. Oh, that's a long time ago. I prayed for them. They used to have Chief British Band. Always prayed. And I prayed for them. They come to me about six months before they gave their affair. Is that right? And they engaged the band.
You must have made quite a bit of money out of that then in those days, right?
Now, after I was married, you understand, she used to run the business for me. I wouldn't be home. I'd be out.
What year were you all married?
All kinds of contracts for me. And she knew just... 94.
She just knew the dates I had and didn't know the dates I didn't have. She killed them dates.

No, 94. She kept track of all the business. 95. Let me ask you this. You said you were about eight years old when you heard your first rag. Well, around that, yes. Did you... It was a band that played it? Was it a regular professional band that played it? No, I never heard no band play it now. Well, now... No. No. Was somebody whistling it? Or singing it? Was somebody singing it or what?

Plenty of people whistling. Plenty of the kids whistling and different things. Now, there used to be an organ grinder. They used to stop at the corner. That's the time they had them organs to throw you on their back, you know. And they had a tune in there. I can't remember that tune. They used to... That tune used to rag the mischief out of it.
Is that right? That organ grinder?

Organ grinder. And brother, them boys around the corner, even kids around the corner, big men, I'm cheeky and I'm... They'd have that organ grinder stand there and give them as high as 50, 60 cents to stay there and play that tune. Is that right? Yeah.

Papa, do you have any idea when professional bands first started playing rags? When bands played the rags? Ragtimes, not rags. Ragtimes. Do you have any idea when they started playing rag times for money? No, I haven't.
Was that before you were born, do you think? No, I was playing music then. I had a ragtime band. And I'm about the first one that ever had a ragtime band on the street.

Is that right? That's correct. The first professional band? First, correct. That's correct. First one. Now, this Dave Perkins did not play ragtime. Dave Perkins did not play ragtime. Oh, yes. Dave played rag.
He used to mix this stuff up. Before you started playing? Oh, yeah. He played. Yeah, he played music. That's how I come to get Dave because Dave and I used to be pretty friends.
I see.

And he used to go see a lady in the block from me, you know. And he was always down by my house all the time. And he was a wonderful musician. Read music. Oh, that boy's heck of a sheet. And really just like nobody's business.
Where were you living in those days? On Charter Street. Charter Street? What number? Do you remember? 24, 2405, wasn't it, Charter?
Yes, sir. Near Manneville?
Yeah, next to the corner of Manneville. Right.
It was a basement house. Mm-hmm. I lived in there for years and years. We used to rehearse it in the basement.
I see.
All the kids get that in the basement. Yeah.
Let me get everything. Right. Papa, who was in your band when you got married about that time? Who was in your band when you got married? When I got married? Mm-hmm.
Manuel Marlowe, Leo Marlowe, Robbie Kirsch, Martin Kirsch, Gussie Zinneman, and the Chinaman, and... Was that King Martin? Yeah. Kit Martin, Vega, Buck A., and the Shields.
So many of them. I couldn't remember. Yeah. Well, do you remember when Dave Hennessy got killed? He was the chief of police? Oh, yes.
Yes.
Well, who was in your band then? My band then?

I had that same band when we was kids. One of us kids, yeah. Same band. Same band as when you were kids? Yeah. Who was that? Playing piccoloos and stuff like that. Oh, yeah. When he killed Steve Hennessy, when he went and got them dagos out of prison, you mean? Yeah. And lynched them. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Young sir, regular young sir, Ed. Mm-hmm. Papa, I want to ask you about that political meeting again. Did you have a name for your band when you played that political meeting? No, just Lane's Band, that's all. Lane's Band. We call it Lane's Band.
We wasn't married by that Dave.
Let's see, what kind of instruments did y'all have for that? Just drums and piccolos? Yes, we had one piccolo. One piccolo.
One piccolo player. And we had clarinet. Clarinet. Trombone. Trombone. Carnet. Alto. Tuba. Tuba. And baritone. Of course, drums, of course. And one piccolo.

One piccolo. Now that again was when you were 15 years old. That was around 15 years old. Yeah. I'll be there. Yes. Mm-hmm. Yes. And none of your music had any name to it. You didn't play any, you didn't know the name of any of the songs you played? Never knew the name. The whole thing was just out of your head.

That's right. That's right. We make up that stuff. We tell you a whole lot of stuff. Just like if we were playing it for years, we'd make it up. Yeah. And we'd fight it out and fight it out until we got some kind of time out of it. Good time out of it, you know. Regular dancing time. For a dance. Perfect. And for a march, had a different time for a march.
Uh-huh.
See?

Were your boys in your band, when you were 15, playing this political meeting, were your boys white or were they colored or were they both? Oh, I never had no colored. All white. All white. I see. Were there any colored bands playing that kind of music then? Not that I know of. Is that right? Not that I know of. As far as you know, the first band that was playing this ragtime was white. No. Is that right?

The first one that I remember was me to come out on the street and play that, play that stuff. But I don't remember any other band. Is that right? No. I don't remember any other band playing that stuff.
Well, what did Billy Braun's band play like? Ask him what Braun's. Braun? Yeah.
Military stuff. Oh. Marches? Marches and stuff like that.
But they did not rag those marches? No.
No. Sentimental music. All straight stuff.
Sentimental music and marches, huh?
But Braun was a musician. I want to tell you that. He could turn his band into a good ragtime band because he knew his business.
Let me ask you this. How long had you been playing for money before Buddy Bolden became well known? Oh, quite a while. Quite a while?
Yes.
How many years? Ten years before Bolden?
I wouldn't... I couldn't say these things unless I was pretty much sure. Sure. You know? I know what you mean?

Well, you know, Papa, you're older than Bolden was, and they always talk about him being the first man. But you're older than him. Buddy Bolden? If he was alive, you'd be older than him. I'd be older than him? Oh, yeah. Yeah, of course I'd be older than Buddy Bolden.
Yeah. Sure. Sure. Sure. If he was alive, even so. He said I was still older than him. Yeah. Yeah.
Ask him about Seaforth's band. Yeah. Seaforth, yeah. How about the Seaforth band? Remember that?
He was a military band, too. Military. That's right. Yeah. He had a good orchestra. He had a good orchestra. They all straight stuff.

What about D.C.? I want to ask him about Bolden one more. Okay. I want to ask you one more about Bolden. How come Buddy Bolden gets all the credit for being the first when you were before Bolden playing ragtime? Okay. Why does he get the credit?
Well, those guys goes up to New York, you understand? I see. And, of course, up there and took what they said for granted.
Uh-huh.
You understand? Right. But-
But to tell you, even so, Buddy Bolton was my age and started out when I started out. That'd be a colored band. That wouldn't be the first white band ever organized a ragtime band. No, no.
We're talking about a ragtime band regardless of color. I'm not thinking about color. Just thinking about the style of music, you know.
Well, that's how it was. That fellas went to New York and all you know. Now, they wrote for me to go up there.
They had.

And I'll tell you, it was one night. How I come not to go up there, it was another political parade I was playing. And I had this man, La Rocca, in the band. Nick La Rocca? He played with me, too. I'd pick up La Rocca when he hardly heard anything about it, Trumper. And I'm playing the music on the street. Some fellas stepped in and was told to me after.
I'll ask Paul. I'll ask Paul.

I want to know who's the leader of the band. I want to get a band to go to New York. La Rocca, give them a note. And this fella goes to La Rocca's house. You see, La Rocca and La Rocca organize a band goes to New York. I see. Unnoticed to me.

Well, this was a long, long time after you first started music. Oh, yes. This was about 1915 or 16. Oh, a long time. A long time after, yeah. Well, let's see. You started playing when you were about 16 years old professionally for money. Yes. And that would have been about 1882, 1883, 1885, something like that. Something along that. About 1887. Well, now, Buddy Bolton did not start playing until about the 1890s, right?
No. No, at that time, no, now. If he did, I never heard of him.
I see. He was not well known. No. I see.
If he did, I never heard of him.
He became well known in the 1890s, I guess.
He ought to.
Yeah. No.
No. At that time, no, I never heard of him. But I knew him. Oh, you did know him?

Yes, I knew him. Did you hear him play much? Yes, I heard him play. Papa, can I talk a while? Yeah. Because the tape's about to run out, and I want to do some talking now while I'm changing the tapes. Okay. Okay. I don't know what I'm going to say, but I'll talk. Yeah, this is a second reel on Papa Lane. I got it going now. It's April the 25th, 1964. Who was Baptiste O'Quinn? I got to get over there, Papa. You can't hear me. Who was Baptiste O'Quinn? Baptiste O'Quinn? Yeah.
Well, I wouldn't know. I wouldn't know who he was, but when I found out he was a nigger, that's when I stopped hiring him.
You stopped hiring Baptiste O'Quinn?

Yeah. When I found out he was a colored boy, I stopped hiring him. I never knew he was colored, but he married a white woman. He's married to a white lady. And I never knew it. But I didn't know that he was a colored boy. Never knew it. One fine day, I passed on Osterlein Street, where he lived. And I saw his daddy. And that was a no.
What did he play? What instrument? Ask him what instrument.
Violin and an alto. An alto. An alto.

Well, he should have been from the Seventh Ward. You know what they call the Seventh Ward? The what? They changed the word line so many times. No, no, no. You know what they call it around St. Bernard Avenue? They call that the Can't Tell Ward. Tell him. I don't still get it. Tell him. Along about St. Bernard Avenue, they call that the Can't Tell Ward, because you can't tell if they're white or colored. What about Paoletti's band? Who? Paoletti. Baoletti? Paoletti. Paoletti. Paoletti. Paoletti. Letty? Paoletti. Paoletti. You don't remember that name? No. No. Don't remember. I see. Dick's going to tell you. Paoletti had a band out at West End, you know, and played on the lakefront. And he'd play around Spanish for it a lot. He had a big band.
Well, I played out there all the time. I had bands out there regular. You played at the West End? Well, I never heard of this band.

What about Almond Vesey? Never heard of him. Never heard of him. They may have been after your time, Papa. Must have been late bands. Must have been. Yeah. It couldn't have been around my time. Papa, let me ask you something. Did you ever go to any colored funeral marches when you were a child? No. Never did go to those colored funerals? No. No.
Never did.
Well, then you don't really know what the colored people were playing when you were growing up. No. I see. No.

Now, we used to play pretty good marches. It was one march we played. Can't think of the name of that march now. Well, anyhow, we used to play it. We played it regular so people would know just the stuff we played. For every funeral, we played it regular. You played at funerals?
Oh, Lord, yes. They had bands at white funerals? Yes. Is that right? Oh, yes. I played many funerals. Is that right?
Yes.

You can tell you that. Well, did they have bands at white funerals when you were a child, when you were a little boy? Yes. Is that right? Yes. When did they stop doing that? When did they stop doing that? When did they stop having bands at white funerals? I wouldn't know. Well, they never have stopped. They always have been military funerals. I never know. Well, I mean, yeah. I wouldn't know. It was a rule, Papa, for all organizations to at that time. I see. All the fraternal organizations throughout the country. It was a rule for all organizations that time to have bands.
Oh, yes. I reckon so. I wouldn't know that.

In my ignorance. You can look it up in the Masonic, you know, the Masons have a book. And it tells you all that. You can go look in the old books, Papa. Papa, you were talking about at this political rally when you were 16 now, your songs did not have any names. No. Now, after that, when you played other jobs, what's the first song you can remember your band playing? Plow Rain. What's that? A song called Plow Rain. Plow Rain. Like Rains for a Horse? No, no. No. Plow Rain is like Pecan Candy.
The name of the call of the plane. Oh, oh. The name of the piece we played. We give it a name. Yeah. Stuff that we bring up ourselves. I see.
Plow Rain.
Yeah. Plow Rain. Plow Rain. Meatballs. And Sunlight. Moonlight on the Shovel. And all that sort of funny names.
Moonlight on the Shovel?
Funny names. Funny names.
Well, who made up those names? Did you make up those names? Yeah, the boy did. With me. Is that right?
Yeah. Not only me myself. Uh-uh.
Plow Rain's Meatball. Yeah. Moonlight on the Shovel. Can you remember any more? No, I can't remember.
But there's lots of them we played, and I can't remember all of them.
Little Bunch of Whiskers on a Young Man Grew.
Tell him. Little Bunch of Whiskers on a Young Man Grew.
Yeah. You remember that one? That's old. Oh, yeah. Tell him I found a record of Kentucky Days yesterday. He found a record of Kentucky Days yesterday. Oh. Yeah.

That was my favorite. Is that right? I'll tell you a little instance that's happened about Kentucky Days. Now, this is a queer thing with our boy, Alfred. I've got three bands in Biloxi. Understand me? Uh-huh. I've got a band for West End Junior, band for West End Fire Company, number three, and a band for volunteer, number one. Okay. It was a park right on the other side of Kennedy's Hotel. Great big park. And there was a military band in this park. And there was a park. And there was a park. And they were sitting all around the mound. And they were talking. And they seen all my kids, a bunch of my kids out. All little fellas. Like the Georgie Brunas, Henny Brunas, and all that bunch. Kids, my boy, you know. Young, young kids. And they seen them walking around, you understand. And they had the uniforms on, see. So, uh, one fella in that bunch of soldier band, military band, he passed a remark. He said, Jesus, look at this. This must be a kindergarten band. I'd like to hear them play. He'd like to hear them play. Well, now that was carried over to me. I was right across the street from the park. See. So, all right. They, uh, they all got together, were ready to leave. To go on a parade. And they struck up any bones, any bottles today.
Is that right? Yeah.

You understand? Uh-huh. I got all the kids together. Play Kentucky Days. When you come to that trill, come down soft. Be sure you do that. They were listening to me, you know. All right. They got around there and they popped them loose. First damn thing you know, them soldiers, when they finished, they took their hats off. Like that was doing that, waving at that kid band. Waving at that kid band. That was the kindergarten band they were going to hear. That's good.

Papa, can I ask you about that political rally again? I'd like to talk about that. You remember anything that happened at that political meeting? No. Remember any of the speeches? Do what? Do you remember any of the speeches or anything that happened at that meeting at all? No.
No.
Just played the rally, that's all. That's right. Could you hum us another couple of tunes that you played at that rally?

Well, I wouldn't remember. You just don't remember. I mean trying to hum them and make a stew out of it. I see. I'd rather not to because I want to be right. I know what you mean. I want to be right. I don't want to say a thing or do a thing unless I know I'm right. Unless I did it or something of that sort. I'm not sure I did it.
You remember where that rally was? What part of town was that rally in?
Well, they left from, I remember that well. They left that rally started from Legion Field in Dauphine. I believe it was in Louis Knops Bar, if I'm mistaken.
That's where the political rally started. Louis Knapp? Huh? Louis Knapp?

No. Yeah. No. No. He can't have no liberal people. I believe it was there. I think it was just thought there. There's a big hall upstairs, I know. There's a hall upstairs. I'm going to get a picture of that. And we played all through the street. All around. Met the bunch up by the Elks place, Elks home. What? The Elks home? Yeah. That's where all them different wards met. Yeah. See? And we went out on the march. After we busted up, that was all.
I see. You got $33 for that. Yeah. Ask him where the Elks home was then. Do you remember where the Elks home was?
Where was the Elks home? That was on Canal, at least Basin. I think Basin near Canal, somewhere along that way.
Yeah. You marched all the way through the quarter then to Basin and Canal.
I see. I believe it was on the right-hand side, I think it was. The right-hand side of Basin Street.

Yeah. Yeah. Now, did you have anybody else in that band who was older than you were? Were there boys who were older than you were? No. No. They were all your age or younger? Yeah, they were. Yeah. Fifteen and sixteen-year-old kids. That's the song.

All children. Now, when William Brunish started to play with me, when I took him to play with Alto, he was eight years old. Is that right? My boy was only eight years old. And Abby Brunish was about a year or two older then. Then Richie was about the same thing, two years or two older. See?
Yeah.

I took them all in the band. And I'll tell you about the Brunish boys. The daddy was a good musicianer, good violin player, mighty good violin player. And he loved music. He sure loved music. That old man sure loved music. So he'd get them kids all together, he's kids, buy them old instruments and stuff, and practice. And get out on the street with them kids. Is that right? On the street and play at the corners. If you give them nickels, all right, if you didn't, it was all right too. That was old man, brother.
Fine old dance. Did you ever play the Lusitanus Hall? Oh my God. Yeah. Where was that at?
Huh? Where was that at? The Lusitanus on Dauphine? Mm-hmm. Yeah.

Yeah. Dauphine, what was the other street that it was on? Dauphine and Lusitanus. Dauphine near what? Near Lusitanus? Lusitanus. Lusitanus. Wasn't it? No. On Dauphine and Lusitanus? Yeah, that's right. Well, that's right near Knob's Bar. Yeah, next to the police station. Where, Lusitanus? Lusitanus. Yeah. That's where we used to be. On Lusitanus. Yeah. That's where we used to be.

That's the way Perkins learned us how to play. Oh, with respect to you, bumps you the rat tail. I forgot the name. I can't figure that. He pumped away with his trombones, that damn pursuing. Boy, he turned the house down.
Is that right?

What kind of style did he play? How would he play? What kind of trombone would he play? How did he sound? What was it like? Pretty good. Yeah, but would he go? No, no. He played the whole melody. Oh, played the whole melody.
Yes, sir. Oh, Perkins was a musician. He carried the lead, huh? Huh? He carried the lead.
Yeah, yeah, carried the lead. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Now, was that the first real musician you had ever been around, Dave Perkins? The first one ever I have been.
You mixed up with your... I see. First one.
Reader. Musicians are readers, you see.

Readers. The first reader, I see. Yeah. And mind you, it turned out that this Dave Perkins was a colored man, too. Is that right? Yeah. But he was passing for white. Is that right? Oh, yes. Uh-huh. He was going to marry a white girl. Oh. In my neighborhood. I see. And somebody put her next to it. Something. Yeah.
Ask him what color hair he had.

What color hair did he have? Straight hair. Straight black? Blonde. Blonde hair. Yeah, he was blonde. Fair as a lily. With blue eyes. Fair as a lily. Blue eyes? Yes. Yes. And let me tell you one thing about that guy. That guy was a good drug clerk. Is that right? Yes, sir.
Papa Lane, let me ask you this. When you were a little boy, when you first started playing, were you from a poor family? Was your family poor when you grew up?
Well, no, not exactly poor. If you want, no. What did your daddy do for a living? My daddy, he was a contractor, working with a contractor. He was a builder?

Yeah. I see. He had a nice home. Is that right? Y'all grew up in a nice home. Yeah. Now, these boys that played in your band at this political rally, were they poor or about like you were? Who's that? Those boys that played at that political rally. They weren't poor boys, were they? The boys that played at that political rally, you know, when you were 15 years old?
15, 16 years old.
Those other boys in that band, now, were they poor or were they about like from the same kind of family you were?
Well, that I couldn't say. I couldn't say. But it looked like their family was pretty well. Pretty well healed.

You'd call them middle class, would you? You would call them middle class? Yeah, I'd call them middle class. I'm asking if they were working. Working people, though. Working people. Working people. I see. Did your daddy own his own home? Did your daddy own his home or did he rent? My daddy? Yes. No, we rent. You rent it. I see. We had a nice home. That's how they could all rehearse, you see. Ask them about those rehearsals.
Oh, that was at our place on Chard and Mandeville. It was a three-story place.
I see.
Where you rehearsal on Chard and Mandeville. That was our home when we lived there. There's where you rehearsal on Chard and Mandeville. That's right. In that basement. That was our home.
Yeah, that was our home. Yes. Well, you must have made good money. I did. I did. Whatever. I sent the two kids to school. Give them high education. All on music.
Is that right?
All on music. Did you go to school? Did you go to school? Did I go to school? Right. I went to school, but not so very much. I see.
When did you leave school?
Oh, I wouldn't have no idea.

Were you still a pretty young... Was that before you started playing for money? Oh, no. It was after. It was after you started playing for money that you left school? Yeah. I see. When did you start making enough money in music to make a living? When did you first start making enough money out of music to make a living? When did I first start? No. When did you first start making good money? When did you first start making good money so you could support yourself out of music?
Well, I'll tell you. I didn't only play music, but I worked on the river.
Yeah, Longshore.

With my brother-in-law. You understand? What kind of work? Longshore. Longshore. My brother-in-law was a boss out there. And whenever I had a job, like tonight, I'd have a job, I'd get off at 12 o'clock today. That's it. That's it, brother? He'd leave me off. That's it, brother? Uh-huh. He'd say, hey, so too. What was his name?
Okay. Smith. He was for the Puerto Rico Steelship Company. He was superintendent.
And I'd play when I'd play them carnival parades and carnival balls. You understand? I had a pay list. It's not long. Is that right?
You used to play this ragtime at carnival balls. Is that right? They liked it, huh?

Oh, they loved it. Uh-huh. They loved it. Yeah. And they'd come down to the house and get their money. All that brothers would come down to the house and get their money. She was my paymaster. I see. When I wouldn't be there or anything, she'd handle all the business. Uh-huh. But they were all right. But when I wouldn't do it, she'd handle all the business. They'd come along there, you know, and stop. If I was there all right, here's your money.

All right. Now, what song did these white people at the carnival balls used to like the most that you played? Which song did they like the most? Most Anything and Everything. There wasn't one particular song they liked?
No. No. No. Well, none in particular. I see. None in particular. In fact, they didn't care what we played. I don't care how we played it or what we played. We got a big hand.
Why was that, do you think? Why did they like you? Why did they like you? Why did you get those big hands?

I don't know. I have no idea. I don't know. They must have liked the music. Could be. They must have liked the music. Otherwise, they wouldn't clap like they did in hollering and whistling and clap on the phone. All that sort of stuff. Play it over.
Play it over.
Play it in core.
Now, did these people used to dance to that ragtime music? Yes. Is it back in the 1880s? In the 1880s? They used to dance with it. How did they dance? Was it kind of a waltz or a...

No, in all kinds. Two steps, shutters, and all like that. Uh-huh. Yeah. But they danced with each other. They didn't dance by themselves. They couldn't dance that stuff with a waltz. I see. See? Two steps. A waltz is different times. Right. See? Six, eight, something like that, you know. See? A different time. Right. They can't dance no ragtime music with a waltz. You couldn't even play ragtime with a waltz.

That's right. When was the last time you played the drums, Papa Lane? When was the last time you played the drums? That was about around the first... first waltz. Well, you played drums since the First World War, haven't you? Didn't you play the drums just a few years ago? A few years ago? Yeah.
Uh-uh.
I don't mean for money. I don't mean in your band. I mean just for fun. When was the last time you played the drums for fun?
Played on tin pan for that, yeah. One day, Bernice has come down to the house, and we organized a bunch of the yard.
Can you play on the table like this? Do you do this much? Yeah. Play something for us. Tip된 stuff with stuff
Oh boy, great.

That's turkey in a straw, isn't it? Yeah. You used to play that, huh? That's a kick, Papa. Papa, let me ask you, what do you, how do you spend your days now? What do you do now? Who? How do you spend your day now? How do I spend my days? Yeah, what do you do during the day? Sleeping and drinking.
Drinking what? What do you drink? I drink whiskey, milk, beer, wine, anything comes along, it's all right.
What do you attribute your old age to, Papa? How come you live to be as old as you are? How come you lasted this long? What's your secret?

Well, now that's a coincidence and a funny thing to answer, funny question to answer. I've been a good boy and a strong boy all my days. I remember being in a kind of serious trouble, nothing of that sort, and I always believed in our Lord. And I brought myself upright. Still, I smoked plenty. I drank plenty. Now, whether it's the whiskey preserved me, I don't know. I couldn't say. It might have been the Lord.
It might have been the Lord.
I played one night up in Protection Levee for Dwyer.
He got good after you.

For Dwyer? For Dwyer up in Protection Levee. And I tell you, they had a car in my home. Is that right? Had a car in my home. And when I got home, I was almost, almost passed out the pitcher entirely. Drinking whiskey? Drinking whiskey? Drinking whiskey. I must have drank a fifth. Oh, that's a lot. I must have drank a whole fifth. Amy and Quigley and that bunch had to carry me. All them kids had to carry me. Really, carry me through the bus and leads the streetcar and from the streetcar home.
What else do you do now besides just drinking and having a good time? What else do you do?
Oh, I'm past my time making them hats now. Now I'm doing it again.
Making those fire hats for the volunteer fire department? Yeah.

You see, those boys over the river, I belong to three fire companies. Uh-huh. See? And them boys over the river, I made them all, about a hundred of them hats. See? They asked me to make some more for them. And they probably might use them around the last of May. See? They said, well, I'll try to do the best I can for you. Well, I've seen them the day of the parade on Canal Street.
Uh, Spring Fiesta.
Is that right? The Spring Fiesta. He was in there.
He was up there.
Is that right? Yeah. They were out too. Oh, I'll be there.
The devil. He can't hardly see. But he goes.
Go get my hat and be, mother.

He goes. My granddaughter, he was going out there. He was sick the other day. And his legs couldn't carry him. And he had his stick in it. She said, I'm a son of a fucker. She said, he'll go if he's got a drop.
Papa, what kind of music do you like the best now? Do you listen to music anymore?
Oh, yes.
What kind do you like to listen to?
All right time stuff.
That's all you listen to?
Jazz stuff. Yeah. Oh, that's something about the stuff I never worried about. I don't know.
You don't listen to any modern music at all? No.
No modern music at all.
Just jazz and ragtime? That's all. You still have some old records that you play here?
Well, I've only got one of my own here. That's all. Uh-huh. What's that record? Papa's Children. Papa's Children. Is that an old one? Yeah. It's a good record. He didn't hear.
He makes them.
Yeah. There's a company I belong to. Paul's Boyd.
1904. That's your number one man in that company, huh?
That's a beautiful hat.
No. No.
Just a bit.
Very nice.
He's exempt from David Crockett.
I can't think of anything else.
Dick, can you think of anything? Yeah, sure. Papa? What about your tent show? Didn't you have your own tent show at one time? Yes. What kind of show was it?
Regular Vortival outfits. What did they do? Sing, dance, do tricks, stuff like that. Regular Vortival.

Papa, let me ask you about your musicians. When you had your band going good back in the 1880s and 1890s, were your musicians pretty good boys? Did they drink all the time? Or were they good family men? Or what kind of men were they?
Oh, pretty good boys. Every one of them. Is that right? Very good. I never had no trouble with none of them buggies. That's right. Pretty good boys. Nice, classic boys. Nice bunch of boys.
They never got arrested or anything like that? No. No trouble with the law?
No.
No mischief? No mischief? Oh, jeez, mischief. You're telling me.
Oh.
Tell us about it. What kind of mischief?
Them kids used to come down to the house in the day. She mothered all of them children. Every doggone one of them.
You mean the boys in your band? The boys in your band? The boys in your band?

The boys in the band. But she's mother of them all. They'd get picked and stuff away around and all. I had a place up stage over the main floor. It was a pretty nice place. They had beds in there where these kids used to come there sometimes at night and sleep. Their mothers used to come to the house and ring up and wonder to find out where was your boy and all that sort of stuff. I'd have to tell them. They're here upstate sleeping or something else. They take the pillars, the feather pillars, and bust them open and throw feathers all around and go. Oh Jesus, give me hell. Oh, they were terrible, mischief. But all fine kids. Every one of them. Fine clipped boys.

Bobby, did you ever live outside New Orleans or have you lived in New Orleans all your life? Do what? Have you lived in New Orleans all your life? Was I here all my life? Yeah. No. Where else did you live? I went to...

Some of my boys took a job up at St. Louis Fair. St. Louis Fair. That's in the 1890s. No, 1904. 1904. I see. Okay. They said for me to come up there. You understand? Uh-huh. And of course I had too many contracts down here, you know, to fill out. So I managed to spend a week up there with them. You understand? And they were playing out near the ground in an artificial palm garden. All artificial plants. Palm garden. Well, it seemed like there was three boys from, I don't know now, I forgot where they're from. They got the job. And they sent for me to bring some men up there. You understand? So I happened to send a fella by name of Tommy Holtz, Tommy Alfred, and George Ulay. Three of them. Mm-hmm. I went up there and them boys learned those fellas. They met the three fellas. A lot about playing music. Is that right? Yeah. I went up there. I enjoyed it. They played up there, oh, a couple of weeks. I'd say, uh, about six or eight weeks. That's how I come to go to St. Louis. I see. I see.
Papa, how did those men know your name, those St. Louis fellas? How did they know your name? They learned it through me. Did...

You see, Alan? Somebody must have told them, or they must have found out who I was, or where they could define me. Then they wrote to me. Asked me to send them, them men. Send them three musicians. See? But they didn't come down here personally. No, no. No, no. They wrote to you. Then I asked them, forward the tickets and I'll send them in. And the tickets. Your tickets, your tickets, tickets off to St. Louis. I wasn't going to send them for that to get the tickets for that St. Louis. Sure. And the return ticket too, mind you. I made that particular business to find that out for you. To and fro. To and fro. That's good.
Did you teach them much when you went up there? Huh? Did you... Could you teach them much when you went up there by doing? No. No. No, I didn't.

I must admit that. No, I didn't. Of course, I spoke plenty about music and watching and understood them, you understand? And there was one... one fellow I can't... Michelle something, funny name, the piano player. He got so interested up there that... Hardy would play the instrument when he's talking to me. He said, talk to me while they're playing. If he's talking to me. Because I didn't know what minute I was going to jump, you know. I had to come back here. Too much work here. I played put in there every night in a week. That's the end of the tape.

segments.title: Opening the tape: date and address
segments.summary: Allen sets up the recorder, dates the tape and asks the address; Blanche gives 421 Hesper.

segments.title: Borrowing Chink Martin's tuba for a Wild West show job
segments.summary: Laine's tuba player falls sick before a Wild West show job, so he borrows Chink Martin's tuba and hands it to a young player, who goes on to become a fine tuba man.

segments.title: Who is older than Laine: Perkins, Baquet, Gilles Rouge
segments.summary: Laine says the old musicians are all dead; he compares ages with Dave Perkins (seven years older), Baquet (his age) and the piccolo player Gilles Rouge.

segments.title: Learning the drums and first paid job at 14
segments.summary: Laine's father bought a field drum around the 1885 Cotton Exposition; he led a kids' field band and played his first paid political parade about two years later.

segments.title: Livery Stable Blues, Baquet and Yellow Nunez, and the Edwards lawsuit
segments.summary: Laine's early band played its own compositions with funny names; he says Baquet and Yellow Nunez made up Livery Stable Blues, which Edwards took credit for in New York and Nunez sued over.

segments.title: What the band played at 14: by ear, marches and dances
segments.summary: Laine and his wife sort out that the Livery Stable Blues era came later; at 14 the boys played by ear, street marches, then orchestra jobs, weddings and balls.

segments.title: Calling it ragtime, and the $33 political parade
segments.summary: Laine says the music was called ragtime; neighborhood kids marched for fun until Dr. George Howard's father hired them for a political parade for $33, with kids following the band.

segments.title: Tunes at the parade, syncopated marches and Dave Perkins's sheet music
segments.summary: Laine can recall only a break and the march 'Underarm' that Perkins brought; they ragged straight marches like Stars and Stripes Forever.

segments.title: First rag heard, cakewalks and what ragtime sounded like
segments.summary: Laine heard his first rag about age eight; he says cakewalks and coon songs came later or weren't played, and Perkins did not teach him.

segments.title: Advance bookings and Blanche running the business
segments.summary: Societies booked Laine's band months ahead; after he married in 1894/95 his wife kept the dates and contracts.

segments.title: The organ grinder and early ragtime tunes
segments.summary: Laine says no band played rag when he was eight, but kids whistled it and an organ grinder's ragged tune was paid for by neighborhood men.

segments.title: Claiming the first ragtime band on the street; Perkins as reader
segments.summary: Laine says he had about the first ragtime band on the street; he recounts how his friend Perkins, a fine reader, came to play with him.

segments.title: The Charter Street basement house and rehearsals
segments.summary: Laine lived at about 2405 Charter near Mandeville in a basement house where the kids rehearsed.

segments.title: Band members at the time of his marriage; the Hennessy killing
segments.summary: Laine lists the men in his band when he married and says it was the same boyhood band at the time of the Hennessy lynching.

segments.title: Instrumentation of the boys' band, no titles, all white
segments.summary: The first band had piccolo, clarinet, trombone, cornet, alto, tuba, baritone and drums, made up tunes with no names, and was all white; Laine knows of no earlier ragtime band.

segments.title: Billy Braun's military band and straight music
segments.summary: Braun's band played marches and sentimental music, not ragged, though Laine says Braun could have made it a good ragtime band.

segments.title: Buddy Bolden and Seaforth's band; why Bolden gets the credit
segments.summary: Laine says he played for money well before Bolden and would be older; Seaforth's band was military; he thinks New York people took the claims for granted.

segments.title: The New York invitation and La Rocca forming a band
segments.summary: Laine was asked to take a band to New York but while he played a parade La Rocca was approached and organized the band that went without him.

segments.title: Bolden: not known to Laine at first, then 'I knew him'
segments.summary: Laine says he never heard of Bolden in the 1880s but then says he knew him and heard him play.

segments.title: Tape change; Baptiste O'Quinn and the color line in hiring
segments.summary: After a reel change Allen asks about Baptiste O'Quinn; Laine says he stopped hiring him on learning he was Black, in a racist account.

segments.title: The 'Can't Tell Ward', Paoletti's band, and Black bands Laine never heard
segments.summary: Allen explains the Seventh Ward and asks about Paoletti and Vesey bands; Laine does not know them and never attended Black funeral marches.

segments.title: Playing at white funerals
segments.summary: Laine's band played a regular march at funerals; Allen notes fraternal organizations were expected to have bands.

segments.title: Funny song names: Plow Rain, Meatballs, Moonlight on the Shovel
segments.summary: Laine lists the made-up titles his boys gave their pieces, such as Plow Rain, Meatballs and Little Bunch of Whiskers.

segments.title: Kentucky Days and the kid band that won over a military band
segments.summary: At Biloxi, soldiers joke about a kindergarten band, then applaud Laine's boys' playing of Kentucky Days.

segments.title: Details of the political rally: route, Knapp's bar, the Elks home
segments.summary: Laine cannot recall speeches or more tunes, but says the rally started near Dauphine and marched to the Elks home on Basin near Canal.

segments.title: The Brunies boys join the band
segments.summary: Laine's band was all young boys; the Brunies brothers joined at about eight to ten, and their violinist father trained them and played on corners.

segments.title: Lusitanus Hall dances and Dave Perkins, the trombonist who passed for white
segments.summary: After locating Lusitanus Hall, Laine praises Perkins as his first reader, playing lead on trombone, and says Perkins was a light-skinned man passing for white.

segments.title: Laine's family and home, rehearsals and schooling
segments.summary: Laine says his father was a contractor and the family rented a nice home; he left school after he began playing for money.

segments.title: Longshore work and carnival parades; Blanche as paymaster
segments.summary: Laine worked on the river through his brother-in-law, who let him off for music jobs; Blanche paid the band.

segments.title: Carnival ball audiences and how they danced ragtime
segments.summary: White carnival audiences loved anything the band played; Laine explains they danced two-steps to ragtime, not waltzes.

segments.title: Playing drums now, on a tin pan and tabletop
segments.summary: Laine says he hasn't played drums for years except on a tin pan and a table, with a turkey-in-the-straw beat.

segments.title: Daily life, drinking and the secret of long life
segments.summary: Laine says he sleeps and drinks, credits good living and the Lord for his age, and recalls a drunken night after playing for Dwyer.

segments.title: Making firemen's hats and the volunteer fire companies
segments.summary: Laine, a member of three fire companies, still makes hats for volunteers and plans to march in the Spring Fiesta.

segments.title: Listening tastes and his own record
segments.summary: Laine listens only to old jazz and ragtime, owns his own record 'Papa's Children' and shows a fire company hat.

segments.title: His tent show
segments.summary: Laine briefly describes his tent show as a vaudeville outfit with singing, dancing and tricks.

segments.title: Behavior of the boys in his bands; Blanche as their mother
segments.summary: Laine says his musicians were good boys; they slept at his house, Blanche mothered them and they got into feather-pillow mischief.

segments.title: Sending three musicians to the 1904 St. Louis Fair
segments.summary: Laine sent three men to a St. Louis Fair palm garden job and spent a week there; he explains how organizers found him and the tape ends.
